Job market paper · Working paper, September 2026 · 87 pages including the Internet Appendix
:::

::: {.standfirst}
Some changes add no information at all: copying a characteristic already in the library, or reweighting a whole theme. On U.S. stocks, even these changes shift which themes a tuned portfolio rule leans on and which stocks it holds. Whether the change helps or hurts depends on the method, the trading costs and how missing returns are valued. Genuinely new characteristics, by contrast, have small and imprecisely estimated effects on forecast accuracy.
:::

## The question {#question}

In the agenda, this is the last step. [Characteristic Geometry](characteristic-geometry.qmd) showed that the ruler's units can move holdings; this paper asks whether the way the library is written can move them too, and follows the answer to named stocks and returns after trading costs.

**If an investment model gets the same information written down differently, does it pick different stocks? And does that change what the investor earns after trading costs?**

**The short answer.** Yes, the stock picks change. Reweighting themes alone, even after the penalty strength is chosen again on past data, makes the positions the two versions want to hold on the same date differ by 19–28% of their average total position size, long plus short <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table I, p. 24">(Table I, p. 24)</span>: a same-date difference in targets, not trading. Whether returns after trading costs rise or fall depends on the method, the cost level and how missing returns are valued.

**Why anything changes: a tax on the square of each bet.** Imagine a tax that grows with the square of every bet you place. Split one bet into five identical smaller bets and the total tax falls to one-fifth: 5 × (b/5)² = b²/5. You would then bet more on that idea, although you learned nothing new. A ridge penalty works this way: five exact copies of a characteristic cut its effective penalty to one-fifth <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, equation 2, p. 5">(Section I.B, eq. 2, p. 5)</span>, so the model leans toward the copied theme.

The analogy has limits. The penalty is a statistical shrinkage device, not a real cost to the investor. Retuning changes one overall tax rate for every theme at once, so it generally cannot undo a split that favoured only one theme <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, p. 5">(p. 5)</span>. The shift is not always harmful: payoff effects differ by method.

## Why it matters {#why}

Library updates are routine, and a better backtest alone cannot tell new information apart from a change in how the estimator weights existing inputs <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.A, p. 4">(Section I.A, p. 4)</span>. Overlap within themes is uneven. The quality theme has 17 measures, but they move together so closely that, in terms of linear overlap, they behave like about 3.5 separate ones (participation rank 3.47). The 12 seasonality measures behave like almost 12 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table II, p. 25">(Table II, p. 25)</span>. This counts directions in the data, not independent sources of information.

- **Economic.** A manager may read a new tilt toward, say, value as news about value; part of it can reflect how many columns represent value.
- **Practical.** Tilts become trades. The original portfolios trade 1.13–1.28 dollars per dollar of capital each month <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table V, p. 28">(Table V, p. 28)</span>, so a change in holdings reaches returns after trading costs.
- **Statistical.** A lower test error does not prove new information. In the paper's simulation, where the information is known, exact copies leave the best achievable (Bayes) error at 0.7500. Yet 16 copies improve retuned ridge's error from 0.7999 to 0.7695 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.C, p. 17; Table VII, p. 30">(Section V.C, p. 17; Table VII, p. 30)</span>.

## The argument at a glance {#map}

::: {.logic-map}
1. **Question.** Does a library change that adds no information still move a tuned rule's holdings and returns after costs? → [The question](#question)
2. **Why.** Library updates are routine, and a better backtest alone cannot tell new information apart from a change in how the estimator weights existing inputs. → [Why it matters](#why)
3. **Framework.** Only the way the library is written changes; data, stocks, dates and method stay fixed, so any response belongs to the fitted procedure. → [The framework](#framework)
4. **Mechanism.** A ridge penalty charges a theme split across m copies only 1/m, and one retuned penalty number generally cannot undo a copy that favours one theme. → [A simple example](#example)
5. **Evidence.** Theme balancing, with no new data, shifts the theme mix of the portfolio's risk by 0.20–0.27 (0 means no change), and the positions the two versions want to hold on the same date differ by 19–28% of their average total position size, long plus short (a same-date difference, not trading) <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table I, p. 24">(Table I, p. 24)</span>. Returns after costs move in method-specific directions; genuinely new characteristics have small, imprecisely estimated forecast effects. → [Design and main results](#results)
6. **Contribution.** A diagnostic that follows a library update to themes, named stocks and returns after trading costs. → [How it relates to prior work](#literature)
7. **Boundary.** No claim of investable profits and no optimal library. → [Scope](#scope)
:::

## The framework {#framework}

The design holds the investment method, the eligible stocks and the decision dates fixed, and changes only how the library is written down <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction, p. 2">(p. 2)</span>. Copying a column adds no new data, and it does not change which portfolios the rule could build <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.A, p. 4">(Section I.A, p. 4)</span>.

**Where the ruler comes in.** To say how much of a stock's expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is; the rule it uses for that is the ruler. Give each characteristic a weight and add them up: every stock gets a score, and the weighted combination is called a direction. The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks, so two value signals that pick out the same cheap stocks overlap under the characteristic ruler but look unrelated under the plain ruler.

**The penalty.** A ridge penalty charges each coefficient by its square, column by column, exactly as the library is written. With m exact copies of a theme, the total charge on a bet on that theme falls to 1/m <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, p. 5">(Section I.B, p. 5)</span>. In stock ridge and blocked ridge every column is charged alike, which is the plain ruler; the Sharpe-weighted variant reweights the columns by their training Sharpe ratios <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.B, p. 11">(p. 11)</span>. This column-by-column charge is not the characteristic ruler, and copying a column is not a change of ruler in the sense of [Characteristic-Space Metrics](characteristic-space-metrics.qmd).

**Themes.** A theme is a group of related measures, such as the 17 quality measures. A **selective copy** repeats every column of one theme, five copies in total. **Theme balancing** rescales each theme's columns by how many columns it has, so that a theme with many columns gets no extra room under the penalty. Like changing units, it adds and removes no information.

The mechanism is one line of algebra: if a characteristic is replaced by $m$ identical columns whose coefficients $\theta_j$ add up to $b$, the cheapest way to split $b$ gives

$$
\min_{\sum_j \theta_j = b} \; \sum_{j=1}^{m} \theta_j^2 \;=\; \frac{b^2}{m}.
$$

<span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, equation 2, p. 5">(Section I.B, eq. 2, p. 5)</span>. For stock ridge there is an exact control: scale the copies' penalty back up (the paper's transported penalty) and the original problem returns <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, p. 5">(Section I.B, p. 5)</span>. Every estimate is mapped back to the 153 original characteristics and scored in the same 13 themes <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.B, p. 12">(Section III.B, p. 12)</span>.

<details class="robustness">
<summary>For specialists</summary>

A library written as $Z_t A$ induces the coefficient penalty $b'(AA')^{-1}b$ <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, p. 5">(Section I.B, p. 5)</span>. The paper measures a coefficient change $d$ by the stock exposures it creates, $d'Q_t d$ (the characteristic ruler), rather than by $d'd$ (the plain ruler) <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.C, equation 3, p. 6">(eq. 3, p. 6)</span>. It warns that a penalty built on the characteristic ruler is not automatically a better investment rule <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.C, p. 6">(p. 6)</span>, and such a penalty (Ridge Gram) forecasts no better in its tests <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table VI, p. 29">(Table VI, p. 29)</span>. Theme attribution uses each theme's share of the fitted payoff's variance, $s_g = \operatorname{Cov}(u_g, u)/\operatorname{Var}(u)$ <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.D, equation 4, p. 6">(Section I.D, eq. 4, p. 6)</span>.

</details>

## A simple example {#example}

{{< include /_includes/_exhibit-helpers.qmd >}}

**Try this.** (1) At k = 1 (no copies), each theme carries 50% of the fitted risk. (2) Drag k, the number of copies of theme X, to 5. Nothing in the data has changed, yet theme X's share rises to 73%. The dashed line uses the same five copies with the penalty scaled back up, and it stays at 50%. (3) Raise λ, the penalty strength, to 4 and the share climbs to about 83%; lower it to 0.1 and it falls to about 55%. (4) Reset λ to 1 and set ρ, how much the two themes overlap, to 0.9: the share reaches about 80%. At moderate overlap it barely moves (about 72–73%), so do not expect a steady rise as you drag ρ. **What to notice:** the copies carry no new information; only the price the penalty charges theme X has changed. λ is held fixed here; in the paper it is re-chosen, and one re-chosen number generally cannot undo a copy that favours one theme <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, p. 5">(Section I.B, p. 5)</span>. Illustrative numbers, not the paper's data.

::: {#figure-jmp-toy .column-body-outset .dfigure .toy role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-jmp-toy-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-jmp-toy-title"><strong>Figure 1: Illustrative example, copying a theme without new information.</strong> Two characteristics, one per theme, equally useful by construction.</div>

{{< include _fig-jmp-toy.qmd >}}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Characteristics X and Z are standardised, overlap by correlation ρ, and each has a true coefficient of 0.5; a ridge rule is fitted to population moments. The last column falls only because this noise-free example has no use for any penalty, so weakening X's penalty lowers the error mechanically. That reflects the penalty, not new information; the paper's simulation shows the same trap with noisy data <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table VII, p. 30">(Table VII, p. 30)</span>. <span class="provenance">Source: computed in the browser from the formulas in Sections I.B and I.D of the paper; no data file.</span></div>
:::

## Design and main results {#results}

The library is the Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen database of 153 U.S. stock characteristics in 13 themes [@jensen2023replication]. The paper follows 179 monthly decisions from January 2011 to November 2025, each estimated on the previous 120 months <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Sections II.A and II.C, pp. 7–9">(Sections II.A and II.C, pp. 7–9)</span>, through four tuned ridge-type portfolio procedures: blocked ridge; a ridge whose penalty is weighted by training Sharpe ratios (Sharpe-weighted ridge), adapted from @ke2025alignment; Universal Portfolio Shrinkage (UPSA), which combines several ridge portfolios [@kelly2026upsa]; and the single ridge rule inside UPSA's public code, chosen by leave-one-out validation (LOO ridge) <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.B, pp. 11–12">(Section III.B, pp. 11–12)</span>. One common rule turns every estimate into stock positions, and stock-by-stock ledgers charge trading costs of 10 to 100 basis points (bp; 1 bp = 0.01 percentage point) per dollar traded <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Sections IV.A and IV.C, pp. 13–14">(Sections IV.A and IV.C, pp. 13–14)</span>.

<details class="robustness">
<summary>Details</summary>

The data are a May 2026 extraction. The allocation rule targets 10% volatility and caps total position size (long plus short) at two dollars per dollar of capital <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.A, p. 13">(Section IV.A, p. 13)</span>. A separate scenario uses a spread-based cost proxy; none includes borrow fees or market impact <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.C, p. 14">(Section IV.C, p. 14)</span>.

</details>

<div class="dfigure-title" id="table-jmp-1-title"><strong>Table 1: Theme balancing changes what all four procedures lean on and hold.</strong> Paper Table I (p. 24), original (O) and theme-balanced (B) libraries.</div>

::: {.table-scroll .tbl-num}
| Method | Attribution change | Holdings change | Sharpe before costs, O | Sharpe before costs, B |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Blocked ridge | 0.231 | 0.277 | 0.366 | 0.348 |
| Sharpe-weighted ridge | 0.198 | 0.239 | 0.490 | 0.397 |
| LOO ridge | 0.271 | 0.227 | 1.003 | 1.105 |
| UPSA | 0.274 | 0.191 | 1.126 | 1.141 |
:::

<div class="figcaption">Attribution change: how far the 13 themes' shares of the portfolio's fitted risk move, half the summed absolute change (0 = no change). Holdings change: the gap between the two sets of stock targets as a share of their average total position size, long plus short (the paper's gross exposure); a same-date difference, not trading. Sharpe ratios are annualised and before trading costs <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table I, p. 24">(Table I, p. 24)</span>. <span class="provenance">Source: Characteristic Libraries and Portfolio Decisions, Table I.</span></div>

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** Rescaling themes adds no data, yet all four procedures change which themes they lean on and which stocks they want to hold, even after the penalty is retuned. Sharpe ratios before trading costs rise for two procedures and fall for the other two <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table I, p. 24">(Table I, p. 24)</span>. So how the library is written down matters, but it does not push performance one way, and a shift in themes is not in itself a loss.
:::

::: {#figure-jmp-cost .column-body-outset .dfigure role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-jmp-cost-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-jmp-cost-title"><strong>Figure 2: Returns after trading costs, at any cost level.</strong> Paper Figure 3 (p. 33), with a cost slider.</div>

{{< include _fig-jmp-cost.qmd >}}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Each panel is one procedure; each line is one version of the library: original, theme-balanced, or five copies of every value characteristic. The vertical axis is the annual mean excess return; held stocks with no next-month return count as zero <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.C, p. 15">(Section IV.C, p. 15)</span>. Exact at 0, 10, 25, 50 and 100 bp; points between are straight-line interpolations. <span class="provenance">Source: Characteristic Libraries and Portfolio Decisions, Figure 3 and Table IV; results file summary.csv.</span> <a href="/data/jmp_cost_sensitivity.json">Data</a></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** Trading costs take most or all of the return before costs. At 25 bp, blocked ridge falls from 2.77% to −0.63% a year and original UPSA from 4.79% to 1.10% <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table IV, p. 27; Section IV.C, p. 14">(Table IV, p. 27)</span>. Under the spread proxy every original portfolio has a negative mean, so returns before costs do not establish a profitable strategy <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table IV, p. 27; Section IV.C, pp. 14–15">(pp. 14–15)</span>.
:::

Library changes then move returns after costs in method-specific directions. For UPSA, balancing changes the mean at 25 bp by −0.19 percentage points; its 95% interval, [−0.57, 0.19], includes zero, so the data cannot tell a gain from a loss <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.D, p. 13">(Section III.D, p. 13)</span>. Of the 52 single-theme copy contrasts at 25 bp, only 2 have simultaneous bands (intervals that hold jointly across a procedure's 13 copy tests) that exclude zero, and both are losses. Five seasonality copies lower the Sharpe-weighted ridge's mean by 1.30 percentage points, band [−2.35, −0.25], and UPSA's by 0.77 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Tables IA.25–IA.27, pp. 77–79">(Tables IA.25–IA.27, pp. 77–79)</span>.

What do genuinely new characteristics add? Adding 114 real characteristics to monthly ridge (from 39 to 153) changes its forecast loss by only 0.0079 percentage points of a zero-forecast benchmark, with a 95% interval from −0.040 to 0.068: the data cannot tell a gain from a loss <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.A, p. 15">(Section V.A, p. 15)</span>. An interval that includes zero does not show that the two libraries forecast equally well <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section VI.A, p. 18">(p. 18)</span>, and the comparison does not separate new information from a change in how strongly the model is penalised <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction, p. 2">(p. 2)</span>. Dropping any single theme does not make forecasts detectably worse once all 13 are tested jointly <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Figure 4, p. 34">(Figure 4, p. 34)</span>. For these procedures on this sample, the differences are small and imprecisely estimated <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.A, p. 16">(Section V.A, p. 16)</span>; that does not mean the added characteristics lack information.

## How it relates to prior work {#literature}

The closest studies compare shrinkage methods on a given library. This paper holds each method fixed and changes only how the library is written down.

::: {.lit-table .table-scroll}
| Prior work | What it established | What this paper adds |
|:--|:--|:--|
| @kozak2020shrinking | Shrinking characteristic-portfolio weights gives stochastic discount factors that hold up out of sample. | Shows that the same kind of penalty responds to how the library is written, down to holdings. |
| @kelly2026upsa | UPSA combines ridge portfolios to target out-of-sample performance and groups weights into economic themes. | Keeps UPSA's public code fixed and changes only its inputs; balancing moves UPSA's theme shares by 0.274 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table I, p. 24">(Table I, p. 24)</span>. |
| @jensen2023replication; @jensen2026implementable | A public library of 153 factors in 13 themes, most of which replicate; portfolios should be judged after trading costs. | Makes that library the object of study and charges costs explicitly; a cost-aware optimiser could change the response <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.A, p. 13">(Section IV.A, p. 13)</span>. |
:::

The controls rest on known identities: duplication invariance [@choueifaty2013properties] and priors that correct for redundant models [@george2010dilution]. Exact copies add no new function, so the paper does not test the broader complexity arguments of @kelly2024virtue and @nagel2025seemingly.

The tools are known; what is new is how much four tuned procedures respond to a change that adds no information, measured on a common U.S. panel and followed to named-stock positions and returns after trading costs <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction, p. 3">(p. 3)</span>. The result is a diagnostic: before adopting a library update, compare attribution, stock targets and returns after costs under the actual implementation, beside an information-preserving control such as exact copies, theme rescaling or, for stock ridge, the transported penalty <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Sections I.B and VI.D, pp. 5, 19">(Sections I.B and VI.D, pp. 5, 19)</span>.

This is the step where the agenda lands. [Geometric Framework](geometric-framework.qmd) and [Characteristic-Space Metrics](characteristic-space-metrics.qmd) choose and qualify the ruler; [Interpreting Pricing Errors](interpreting-pricing-errors.qmd) reads the model's alpha with the ruler held fixed; [Characteristic Geometry](characteristic-geometry.qmd) shows that the ruler's units can move holdings. This paper cites Characteristic-Space Metrics and Characteristic Geometry as companion papers.

## Scope {#scope}

- No claim of investable performance: under the spread proxy every original portfolio has a negative mean <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table IV, p. 27">(Table IV, p. 27)</span>. Original UPSA's mean before fees is 4.79%; valuing held stocks with missing returns at +100% or −100% instead gives 0.62% to 8.98%. These are scenarios, not bounds <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.C, p. 15">(Section IV.C, p. 15)</span>.
- No optimal library: theme balancing is a declared alternative weighting, and the experiment shows neither that it is optimal nor that a uniquely correct metric exists <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction, p. 3">(p. 3)</span>.
- No claim that the added characteristics lack information <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section VII, p. 20">(Section VII, p. 20)</span>.
- The data are a retrospective U.S. extraction that was also used to develop the design, which was not preregistered <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Sections II.F and VI.D, pp. 10, 19">(Sections II.F and VI.D, pp. 10, 19)</span>.
- Intervals condition on the fitted decisions, and an interval that contains zero does not establish equivalence <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section VI.A, pp. 17–18">(Section VI.A, pp. 17–18)</span>.
